To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the BRCA1 mutational spectrum of BC in Sudan is characterized by a high fraction of mutations with inter-continental and uniquely African frequency distribution, 2) the vast majority of BRCA1 mutations in Sudanese patients is neutral or of unknown significance, and 3) the novel missense variant c.Cys1697Tyris predicted to affect phosphopeptide recognition and may have a deleterious effect on BRCA1 function.
BRCA1 mutations are common in Central Sudanese pre-menopausal breast cancer cases, and that the majority of these mutations are of unknown significance.
BRCA1 point variants, including 2 novel missence variants, are present in 59 Central-Sudanese premenopauls breast cancer patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of BRCA1 point variants and their potential clinical impact in a population from a low-resource rural African setting.

the characterization of BRCA1 variants in premenopauls breast cancer from Central Sudan, with particular focus on variants with African distribution, and with the identification of a novel deleterious variant.
the identification of BRCA1 mutations in premenoapusal BC patients from Central Sudan and with the characterization of their potential pathogenicity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BRCA1 mutations in premenopause BC from Sudan are not yet well understood, but that they are likely to be a major factor contributing to disease occurrence.

the BRCA1 point mutation spectrum in premenopauls breast cancer patients in Central Sudan is similar to that reported in other African countries, and is characterized by a high frequency of mutations with unique African or intercontinental distribution.
the BRCA1 variants reported here do not represent a major cause of hereditary predisposition to BC in the Central Sudanese women studied.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the high genetic heterogeneity of the Sudanese population and the high frequency of rare or unique mutations, may be responsible for the high incidence of BC in Central Sudan.

, in Central Sudan, the majority of BRCA1 mutations in premenopause BC patients is neutral, while a minority is potentially deleterious, with a high fraction of mutations with inter-continental and uniquely African frequency distribution.
the BRCA1 mutational profile of Central Sudanese BC patients, as well as the BRCA1 mutation spectrum in African women in general, remains largely to be elucidated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
BRCA1 mutations are common in Central Sudan and are likely to contribute significantly to BC risk in this population.

BRCA1 genetic testing should be tailored to the local genetic background and should be performed in a context where the clinical relevance of variants is assessed by a multidisciplinary team.
